To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
time-lapse anomalous diffraction shows how ferritin protein nanocrystal cages bind and move ferrous ions to enzyme sites in the cage to initiate biomineralization.

the crystal structures of ferritin M from R. catesbeiana show the Fe(2+), O2, O2- and O3- substrate ions entering, binding and moving through the protein cages, with the Fe(2-) and O3- ions moving along the threefold symmetry axes and the O2 and O2- ions binding at the fourfold symmetry axes.

the time-lapse crystal structures of ferritin show how Fe(2+), O2 and H2O2 substrates bind at enzyme sites to synthesize internal Fe2O3 ·H2O biominerals in the protein cages of the ferritin superfamily, and that the Fe(2+)-substrate binding sites are located in the cage at the oxidoreductase centres and ion channels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of ferritin biomineralization and the structural basis for the enzyme activity of ferritin.
the biomineralization of ferritin protein nanoscale cages and the mechanism of the iron storage and release process, and it provides a unique insight into the mechanism of ferritin biomineralization.
the mechanism of iron oxidation in the cage and the movement of the iron substrate from the cage interior to the cage exterior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ferritin protein cage acts as a bioreactor for the synthesis of Fe(2)O(3)·H(2)O.
the ferritin superfamily protein cage is a dynamic nanoreactor that reversibly and efficiently synthesizes internal biominerals.

the ferritin superfamily protein nanocages reversibly synthesize and store biominerals by using the Fe2O3 nanocluster as the active site for the enzymatic oxidation of ferrous ions and the Fe2O4 nanocluster as an intermediate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the time-resolved structures of ferritin protein cages show the movement of Fe(2+) ions through the cages to the oxidoreductase centres and other binding sites, and that the Fe(3+)(O2)2 complex is the likely product of the enzymatic cycle.
the ferritin protein nanoscaffolds are able to bind, transport and concentrate Fe(2+) ions, and then to synthesize the Fe2O3 nanoclusters in the cage interior.
the ferritin protein cage acts as a nanoreactor, and that the cage structure is dynamic in the presence of the Fe(3+), O2, Fe(2+) substrates, as well as in the absence of these substrates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the protein cage can be viewed as a molecular machine that reversibly synthesizes and stores biominerals.
ferritin superfamily protein nanocages are dynamic structures, and their internal biomineralization reactions involve a series of intermediate steps.

the crystal structures of ferritin protein cages with different iron-binding sites occupied by the Fe(2+)-substrate ions provide snapshots that show how iron substrates move from the protein cage surface to the oxidoreductase site and then to the biomineralization site.
